title: The 3 Secrets of Making Your Ideas Rejection-Proof
author: Nir Eyal
summary: Nir Eyal recaps an Essentials for the Busy Mind author session with Dan Pink on the science of persuasion, organised around three reader questions. First, extroversion is not required: Pink points to research that the best salespeople are often ambiverts, and advises extroverts to ask more questions and let people finish, while introverts can stretch toward the middle. Second, persuading someone who resists starts with attunement, the ability to step out of your own head and learn what drives the other person's position, illustrated by Pink's daughter asking hesitant parents what they have heard before offering evidence. Third, recovering from a no means treating setbacks as temporary, specific and not personal, using self-compassion and self-distancing by asking what you would tell a friend in the same position. Eyal's takeaway is that persuasion works best when it grows from understanding, clear communication and resilience after rejection. The final section is a promotion for the program, which is not part of the argument.
points: Persuasion is not the preserve of extroverts; ambiverts do best, and extroverts can improve by asking more and talking less.
Effective persuasion begins with attunement and curiosity about what is driving the other person's position, not a stronger argument.
Rejection should be treated as temporary, specific and not personal, with self-compassion rather than harsh self-criticism.
Self-distancing, asking what you would tell a best friend in the same situation, is a simple problem-solving heuristic after a setback.
quotes: Maybe make fewer statements and ask more questions. Maybe let the person finish actually talking, take a two-second break and then respond.
Being persuasive isn’t about becoming the loudest person in the room. Sometimes, the most persuasive thing you can do is stop talking long enough to understand someone else.
Pink argues that effective persuasion starts with attunement, the ability to get out of your own head and understand the other person’s perspective.
The way to sell effectively is to become more and more human.
We tend to think persuasion means making an even stronger argument, but sometimes we need to put our protests aside and practice curiosity about what’s driving the other person’s position.
Treat yourself with kindness rather than contempt. Recognize that mistakes and setbacks are part of the human condition. And also that this one moment of setback is a tiny segment of life.
If your best friend was in the situation, what would you tell him or her? That’s actually one of the best problem-solving heuristics there is.
The better we are at seeing what matters to the other person, communicating clearly, and staying resilient after rejection, the better we are at moving people.
